\chapter{Two Things at Once}
\label{ch:ur-two-things-at-once}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put two nouns in one sentence with \ur{اور}, offer a choice with \ur{یا}, turn a clause against the one before it with \ur{لیکن}, and agree with somebody using \ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہے}.}

The chapter-15 practice line bārish, dhūp, aur hawā -- which asked the learner to say a word the book had never taught -- is said with every word owned, then re-joined as a choice and refused twice over.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aur]{\ur{اور} (aur) — and}

\label{lesson:UR-C20-aur}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter gave you a way to refuse two things at once. There has never been a way to accept two things at once.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the double refusal — \emph{na pānī, na hawā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{اور}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{پانی} \ur{اور} \ur{ہوا}} — \emph{pānī aur hawā} — \textbf{water and air.}
\end{quote}

\emph{bārish aur hawā}, rain and wind, is the same shape: the first noun's letters are still ahead of you in the script ladder, so it is printed in romanization.

Chapter fifteen already asked you to say this. Its practice line reads \emph{bārish, dhūp, aur hawā} — and the book had never taught \textbf{\ur{اور}}, so the learner was told to say a word they had never met and could not read. This lesson pays that back.

Three letters, all of them yours: \textbf{\ur{ا}}, \textbf{\ur{و}}, \textbf{\ur{ر}}. The middle one is the \emph{vāʾo} of chapter eight, doing its vowel job.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{اور}} is inherited, not borrowed — Sanskrit \emph{aparam}, \textquotedblleft{}the other one, the further one,\textquotedblright{} worn through Prakrit into one syllable. The counting sense is still there when the word stands alone in front of a noun: \textbf{\ur{اور} \ur{پانی}} means \emph{more water}, not \emph{and water}. Bengali's \emph{ār} is the same word by the same road, which is the sort of relative Urdu's Persian layer usually hides.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bārish aur hawā}
  \item the chapter-fifteen line, this time knowing every word — \emph{bārish, dhūp, aur hawā}
  \item \emph{pānī aur dūdh} — water and milk
  \item \emph{aur pānī} — and hear it mean \emph{more water}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{\ur{اور}} mean before it meant \emph{and}? (\textbf{More, the other one} — Sanskrit \emph{aparam}.) What does it mean standing alone before a noun? (\textbf{More}.) And which word refuses the two things \textbf{\ur{اور}} joins? (\textbf{\ur{نہ}}, doubled.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yā]{\ur{یا} (yā) — or}

\label{lesson:UR-C20-ya}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{اور}} gives somebody both things. Nothing in this book has ever made anybody choose.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the joiner from the lesson before — \emph{aur}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{یا}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{پانی} \ur{یا} \ur{ہوا}} — \emph{pānī yā hawā} — \textbf{water or air.}
\end{quote}

And with a noun whose letters are still ahead of you, in romanization: \emph{pānī yā dūdh}, \textbf{water or milk}.

Two letters — \textbf{\ur{ی}} and \textbf{\ur{ا}} — and it sits exactly where \textbf{\ur{اور}} sits, between the two things. Nothing else in the sentence changes.

The word hides inside one you already read every day: \textbf{\ur{کیا}}, \emph{what}, ends in these same two letters, and every raw search for \textbf{\ur{یا}} in the first eighteen chapters of this book turned up that tail and nothing else. The word was everywhere on the page and nowhere in the book.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{یا}} is Persian, taken whole. Urdu's two ordinary coordinators come from opposite directions — \textbf{\ur{اور}} inherited from Sanskrit through Prakrit, \textbf{\ur{یا}} borrowed from Persian — and a learner uses them in the same breath without noticing the seam. That seam is the language.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pānī yā dūdh}
  \item the same pair joined instead of split — \emph{pānī aur dūdh}
  \item \emph{chāy yā dūdh} — tea or milk
  \item it as an offer — \emph{kyā āp chāy yā dūdh leṅge?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which joiner adds and which one chooses? (\textbf{\ur{اور}} adds; \textbf{\ur{یا}} chooses.) Which of the two is inherited and which borrowed? (\textbf{\ur{اور}} inherited from Sanskrit; \textbf{\ur{یا}} borrowed from Persian.) And which word already on every page ends in the same two letters? (\textbf{\ur{کیا}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lekin]{\ur{لیکن} (lekin) — but}

\label{lesson:UR-C20-lekin}



\begin{quote}
Two joiners so far. One adds, one chooses, and neither of them can disagree with anything.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the two items before this one — \emph{aur}, \emph{yā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{لیکن}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{پانی} \ur{ہے،} \ur{لیکن} \ur{ہوا} \ur{نہیں}} — \emph{pānī hai, lekin hawā nahīṅ} — \textbf{there is water, but no air.}
\end{quote}

And with the two clauses chapters four and nineteen taught, whose verbs carry letters still ahead of you in the script ladder: \emph{maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ, lekin maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā} — \textbf{I am well, but I do not understand.}

\textbf{\ur{اور}} puts two clauses on the same side. \textbf{\ur{لیکن}} turns the second one against the first. It stands at the head of the clause it turns, after a comma in writing and after a small drop of the voice in speech.

Four letters, and every one of them is already yours: \textbf{\ur{ل}}\ur{،} \textbf{\ur{ی}}\ur{،} \textbf{\ur{ک}}\ur{،} \textbf{\ur{ن}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{لیکن}} is Arabic \emph{lākin}, and there is a negator inside it: Arabic \emph{lā}, \textquotedblleft{}not,\textquotedblright{} plus an old particle. English did the same thing by a different road — \textbf{but} is Old English \emph{be-ūtan}, \textquotedblleft{}be \textbf{out}, except.\textquotedblright{} Two unrelated languages built their adversative out of a word for leaving something aside.

Urdu has a second word for \emph{but}, \emph{magar}, which is Persian and slightly more literary. Its middle letter has no lesson in the script ladder yet, so it is named here and left in romanization; \textbf{\ur{لیکن}} is the one to reach for anyway.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ, lekin maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā}
  \item the same two clauses with the other joiner — \emph{maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ aur maiṅ samajhtā hūṅ}
  \item and hear what changed — the second clause no longer argues
  \item \emph{pānī hai, lekin chāy nahīṅ} — there is water, but no tea
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is buried inside \textbf{\ur{لیکن}}? (\textbf{Arabic \emph{lā}, \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}}.) Which English word was built the same way? (\textbf{But}, from \emph{be-ūtan}, \textquotedblleft{}be out.\textquotedblright{}) And what does \textbf{\ur{لیکن}} do that \textbf{\ur{اور}} cannot? (\textbf{Turn the second clause against the first}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭhīk hai]{\ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہے} — all right}

\label{lesson:UR-C20-thik-hai}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ٹھیک}} has meant \emph{fine} since chapter four, and only ever about your health. It has a second life, and it needs one more word.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the joiner from the lesson before — \emph{lekin}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہے}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہے}} — \emph{ṭhīk hai} — \textbf{all right; that's right; agreed.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہے،} \ur{لیکن} …} — \emph{ṭhīk hai, lekin …} — \textbf{all right, but …}
\end{quote}

The copula of chapter two, \textbf{\ur{ہے}}, does all the work. \emph{ṭhīk hai} is what a speaker says to accept a plan, to agree with a claim, and to end a phone call — one phrase covering everything English spreads across \emph{okay}, \emph{fine}, \emph{right} and \emph{deal}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: agreeing, and taking it back}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{said} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
\emph{ṭhīk hai} & agreed \\
\emph{ṭhīk nahīṅ hai} & that is not right \\
\emph{ṭhīk hai, lekin …} & agreed as far as it goes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The middle row is the negator of the last chapter dropped in front of the copula, which is exactly where chapter nineteen said it goes. The third row is the shape almost every real disagreement takes: accept first, then turn.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ṭhīk hai}
  \item \emph{ṭhīk nahīṅ hai}
  \item the half-agreement — \emph{ṭhīk hai, lekin …}
  \item the one-word answers it replaces — \emph{jī hāṅ} … \emph{nahīṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What word does \textbf{\ur{ٹھیک}} need to become an agreement? (\textbf{\ur{ہے}}, the copula from chapter two.) How do you disagree with it? (\textbf{Put \ur{نہیں} in front of the copula} — \emph{ṭhīk nahīṅ hai}.) And what does \emph{ṭhīk hai, lekin …} do that a flat \emph{nahīṅ} does not? (\textbf{Accepts first, and then turns}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aur · yā · lekin]{Two things at once}

\label{lesson:UR-R20-joined-and-turned}



\begin{quote}
Three joiners landed in this chapter. Name them, and say for each one whether it adds, chooses, or turns.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the chapter-fifteen line, whole — \emph{bārish, dhūp, aur hawā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same three as a choice — \emph{bārish yā dhūp}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all three refused — \emph{na bārish, na dhūp, na hawā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the half-agreement — \emph{ṭhīk hai, lekin …}
  \item \emph{Recall:} five lessons back, the question this book learned to ask — \emph{kyā āp ṭhīk haiṅ?}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — every noun in the book, two at a time}
This is what the chapter actually bought. Chapters eight to eighteen taught thirty-odd nouns that could only ever be named one at a time, and every one of them is now combinable. Go back and take them two at a time, cold, from memory — most of these were taught between twenty and sixty lessons ago and have not been asked for since.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item two foods joined, then the same two as a choice — \emph{pānī aur chāy} … \emph{dūdh yā roṭī}
  \item two colours, and mind the agreement — \emph{kālā aur nīlā}, \emph{lāl aur safed}
  \item two garments, then two refused — \emph{qamīz aur jūtā} … \emph{na ṭopī, na koṭ}
  \item two people, then the word that holds them all — \emph{bhāī aur bahan} … \emph{dost aur khāndān}
  \item the face, four parts at once — \emph{kān, nāk, āṅkh aur muṅh}
  \item the one that is not on the face — \emph{dil}
  \item heat against cold, joined and then chosen — \emph{garmī aur sardī} … \emph{garmī yā sardī}
  \item three from chapter eighteen — \emph{ām, āsmān aur purānā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of this chapter's joiners is inherited and which two are borrowed? (\textbf{\ur{اور}} inherited; \textbf{\ur{یا}} from Persian, \textbf{\ur{لیکن}} from Arabic.) Which one can disagree? (\textbf{\ur{لیکن}}.) And what turns any of these sentences into a question? (\textbf{\ur{کیا} at the front}, and nothing else moved.)
\end{tcolorbox}
